power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: You described effects with terms related to 'marginally significant'. If *p* values above 0.05 are interpreted as an effect, you inflate the alpha level, and increase the Type 1 error rate. If a *p* value is higher than the prespecified alpha level, it should be interpreted as a non-significant result. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "Consequently, although individual analytical approaches produced significant coefficients, the evidence taken as a whole did not support reliable prospective relationships between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits.", "Section Header" = "Results"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate at which non-significant p-values are interpreted as marginally significant, see: Olsson-Collentine A, van Assen MALM, Hartgerink CHJ (2019). “The Prevalence of Marginally Significant Results in Psychology Over Time.” Psychological Science, 30, 576–586. doi:10.1177/0956797619830326. For the list of terms used to identifify marginally significant results, see this [blog post by Matthew Hankins](https://web.archive.org/web/20251001114321/https://mchankins.wordpress.com/2013/04/21/still-not-significant-2/). :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.952", Sentence = "When applied to simulated burnout and neuroticism data, the model shown in Figure 2 reproduced the observed correlation matrix exceptionally well (χ² = 0.34, DF = 3, p = 0.952; CFI = 1.000; TLI = 1.007; RMSEA = 0.000, 90% CI [0.000, 0.000])."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports

Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. text.text: Using cross-lagged panel models, Fukuzaki and Iwata reported longitudinal associations between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits.
However, statistically significant cross-lagged coefficients do not necessarily indicate genuine prospective influence because comparable patterns may emerge from other data-generating mechanisms.

We generated simulated data matching the sample size and correlational structure reported by Fukuzaki and Iwata and evaluated the robustness of their findings across several defensible analytic specifications.
Results varied markedly across models.
Some specifications yielded positive prospective associations, whereas others produced negative or non-significant estimates.
When the findings from all specifications were integrated using meta-analytic techniques, none of the overall effects differed significantly from zero.
Consequently, the available evidence appears insufficient to support strong claims regarding reciprocal prospective influences between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits.

Consistent with recommendations from the multiverse-analysis literature, inferences should be based on the pattern of results across reasonable analytic alternatives rather than on the outcome of a single model.

In a longitudinal study of 500 Japanese employees (mean age = 45.9 years, SD = 11.9; 40% women), Fukuzaki and Iwata (2027) examined associations between work engagement, burnout (BO), and personality traits across two assessments separated by one year.
text.formatted: In a longitudinal study of 500 Japanese employees (mean age = 45.9 years, SD = 11.9; 40% women), <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Fukuzaki and Iwata (2027)</ref> examined associations between work engagement, burnout (BO), and personality traits across two assessments separated by one year.

text.text: Based on cross-lagged panel analyses, they argued that burnout may leave "scar" effects on personality and suggested that burnout and neuroticism participate in a self-reinforcing cycle, whereby individuals with elevated neuroticism are more likely to develop burnout, which then contributes to further increases in neuroticism.

Although cross-lagged panel models are commonly employed to investigate developmental and longitudinal processes, significant cross-lagged coefficients should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of prospective influence.
Methodological work has demonstrated that such coefficients may arise even in the absence of direct effects between variables (Campbell & Kenny, 1999; Sorjonen et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Methodological work has demonstrated that such coefficients may arise even in the absence of direct effects between variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Campbell & Kenny, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Sorjonen et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Shared causes, measurement-related factors, and statistical artifacts can all generate longitudinal associations resembling causal effects.
Therefore, statistical significance alone provides only limited support for claims regarding prospective influence.
The present study revisited the conclusions drawn by Fukuzaki and Iwata.
Our objective was to determine whether the reported associations remain stable across a set of plausible analytic approaches.
If conclusions depend strongly on analytical decisions, confidence in proposed prospective relationships should be reduced.
A simulated dataset was created to match the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Fukuzaki and Iwata.
The original data were not available, and a request for access was unsuccessful.

Because adjusted regression estimates are determined by the relationships among variables, analyses based on data reproducing the reported correlation structure should provide a close approximation to analyses based on the original dataset.

Following methodological demonstrations and recommendations provided by Sorjonen et al. (2025 Sorjonen et al. ( , 2026a Sorjonen et al. ( , 2026b)), we estimated prospective relations using three alternative specifications.
text.formatted: Following methodological demonstrations and recommendations provided by <ref type="bibr">Sorjonen et al. (2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Sorjonen et al. ( , 2026a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Sorjonen et al. ( , 2026b))</ref>, we estimated prospective relations using three alternative specifications.

text.text: The first approach examined whether one variable predicted change in another while controlling for the initial level of the outcome variable.
This specification corresponds to the conventional cross-lagged framework and yields coefficient a1 (Equation 1).

The second approach assessed the same relationship while adjusting for the follow-up value of the outcome instead of its baseline value, producing coefficient b1 (Equation 2). Campbell and Kenny (1999) recommended this specification as a means of evaluating potential regression artifacts.
text.formatted: The second approach assessed the same relationship while adjusting for the follow-up value of the outcome instead of its baseline value, producing coefficient b1 (Equation <ref type="formula">2</ref>). <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Campbell and Kenny (1999)</ref> recommended this specification as a means of evaluating potential regression artifacts.

text.text: The third approach estimated the association without controlling for either the baseline or follow-up value of the outcome variable, producing coefficient c1 (Equation 3).
text.formatted: The third approach estimated the association without controlling for either the baseline or follow-up value of the outcome variable, producing coefficient c1 (Equation <ref type="formula">3</ref>).

text.text: The coefficients a1, b1, and c1 represent different operationalizations of the same underlying prospective association.

To derive an overall assessment, estimates from all three specifications were combined using meta-analytic procedures designed for dependent estimates derived from the same dataset (Bartoš et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To derive an overall assessment, estimates from all three specifications were combined using meta-analytic procedures designed for dependent estimates derived from the same dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bartoš et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This approach is consistent with the multiverse-analysis framework proposed by Steegen et al. (2016).
text.formatted: This approach is consistent with the multiverse-analysis framework proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Steegen et al. (2016)</ref>.

text.text: Analyses were conducted in R version 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026) using the MASS (Venables & Ripley, 2002), metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010), and lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) packages.
text.formatted: Analyses were conducted in R version 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026) using the MASS <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Venables & Ripley, 2002)</ref>, metafor <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref>, and lavaan <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref> packages.

text.text: Microsoft Copilot was used for text editing, and the authors approved the edited version of the manuscript.
The correlation matrix and Figure 1.

Both effects of WE/BO on subsequent change in the traits (panel column 1) and vice versa (column 2) are reported.
In each panel, effect 1 corresponds to models adjusting for the initial outcome score (a1 in Equation 1).
text.formatted: In each panel, effect 1 corresponds to models adjusting for the initial outcome score (a1 in Equation <ref type="formula">1</ref>).

text.text: Effect 2 corresponds to models adjusting for the later outcome score (b1 in Equation 2).

text.text: Effect 3 corresponds to models without adjustment for either outcome score (c1 in Equation 3).

text.text: Effect 4 represents the random-effects meta-analytic summary based on all three estimates. analysis scripts are publicly available at GitHub: https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.45_Scar.
text.formatted: Effect 4 represents the random-effects meta-analytic summary based on all three estimates. analysis scripts are publicly available at GitHub: <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.45_Scar">https://github.com/KimmoSorjonen/26.45_Scar</ref>.

text.text: Analyses controlling for baseline levels of the outcome variable (effects with number 1 in Figure 1) closely replicated the conclusions reported by Fukuzaki and Iwata.
text.formatted: Analyses controlling for baseline levels of the outcome variable (effects with number 1 in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>) closely replicated the conclusions reported by Fukuzaki and Iwata.

text.text: For example, greater work engagement predicted subsequent increases in openness (Figure 1, panel I).
text.formatted: For example, greater work engagement predicted subsequent increases in openness (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panel I).

text.text: Burnout predicted later increases in neuroticism (Figure 1, panel K) and decreases in extraversion (Figure 1, panel M), agreeableness (Figure 1, panel Q), and openness (Figure 1, panel S).
text.formatted: Burnout predicted later increases in neuroticism (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panel K) and decreases in extraversion (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panel M), agreeableness (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panel Q), and openness (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panel S).

text.text: In the reverse direction, higher neuroticism was associated with subsequent increases in burnout, whereas higher conscientiousness predicted decreases in burnout (Figure 1, panels L and P).
text.formatted: In the reverse direction, higher neuroticism was associated with subsequent increases in burnout, whereas higher conscientiousness predicted decreases in burnout (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panels L and P).

text.text: A markedly different pattern emerged when follow-up outcome levels were controlled instead (effects with number 2 in Figure 1).
text.formatted: A markedly different pattern emerged when follow-up outcome levels were controlled instead (effects with number 2 in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Under this specification, associations changed direction.
As an example, the positive association between burnout and later neuroticism became negative, and the corresponding effect in the opposite direction likewise reversed (Figure 1, panels K and L).
text.formatted: As an example, the positive association between burnout and later neuroticism became negative, and the corresponding effect in the opposite direction likewise reversed (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panels K and L).

text.text: When neither baseline nor followup outcome values were included as control variables (effects with number 3 in Figure 1), almost all associations failed to reach statistical significance (the sole exception was the association shown in Figure 1, panel D).
text.formatted: When neither baseline nor followup outcome values were included as control variables (effects with number 3 in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>), almost all associations failed to reach statistical significance (the sole exception was the association shown in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, panel D).

text.text: These findings indicate that both the direction and magnitude of estimated prospective effects were highly dependent on model specification.
To evaluate the overall pattern, all estimates were synthesized using meta-analysis.
None of the resulting pooled effects were statistically distinguishable from zero (effects with number 4 in Figure 1).
text.formatted: None of the resulting pooled effects were statistically distinguishable from zero (effects with number 4 in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Consequently, although individual analytical approaches produced significant coefficients, the evidence taken as a whole did not support reliable prospective relationships between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits.
An alternative interpretation of the observed longitudinal associations is presented in Figure 2.
text.formatted: An alternative interpretation of the observed longitudinal associations is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>.

text.text: In this model, repeated measures of burnout and neuroticism are explained by the Spurious Prospective Associations Model (SPAM; Sorjonen, Melin, & Nilsonne, 2025).
text.formatted: In this model, repeated measures of burnout and neuroticism are explained by the Spurious Prospective Associations Model (SPAM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Sorjonen, Melin, & Nilsonne, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The model contains no direct cross-lagged effects between the constructs.
Instead, apparent prospective associations arise because both constructs are influenced by stable general factors as well as a broader higher-order dimension, such as general negativity.

When applied to simulated burnout and neuroticism data, the model shown in Figure 2 reproduced the observed correlation matrix exceptionally well (χ² = 0.34, DF = 3, p = 0.952; CFI = 1.000; TLI = 1.007; RMSEA = 0.000, 90% CI [0.000, 0.000]).
text.formatted: When applied to simulated burnout and neuroticism data, the model shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref> reproduced the observed correlation matrix exceptionally well (χ² = 0.34, DF = 3, p = 0.952; CFI = 1.000; TLI = 1.007; RMSEA = 0.000, 90% CI [0.000, 0.000]).

text.text: These findings demonstrate that the pattern interpreted by Fukuzaki and Iwata as evidence of prospective influence can be accounted for without specifying any direct longitudinal pathways.
Moreover, the SPAM framework provides a potential explanation for why different analytic specifications produced, as reported above, positive, negative, and null estimates of prospective effects.
The present reanalysis revisited evidence that Fukuzaki and Iwata interpreted as indicating reciprocal longitudinal relationships between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits.
The results revealed substantial sensitivity to modeling decisions.
The conventional cross-lagged approach largely reproduced the original findings, but alternative yet defensible specifications either reversed the observed associations or eliminated them altogether.
Furthermore, meta-analytic integration of all estimates failed to reveal any significant overall effects.
These findings suggest that the conclusions of Fukuzaki and Iwata may reflect dependence on a particular analytical strategy rather than robust evidence of prospective influence.

Additional support for this interpretation comes from the SPAM shown in Figure 2, which successfully reproduces the observed correlational structure without requiring direct longitudinal effects between constructs.
text.formatted: Additional support for this interpretation comes from the SPAM shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>, which successfully reproduces the observed correlational structure without requiring direct longitudinal effects between constructs.

text.text: Although the present analyses do not demonstrate that prospective influences are absent, they indicate that the available data do not uniquely support their existence.
Researchers should avoid drawing strong causal or quasi-causal conclusions from observational longitudinal analyses alone.
Cross-lagged B B B 2 2 0.3 0.3 0.4 0.4 0.0.
coefficients, like other regression-based estimates, may be generated by several distinct underlying processes.

In line with the multiverse perspective articulated by Steegen et al. (2016), future studies should evaluate hypotheses across multiple defensible analytical specifications and integrate the resulting evidence.
text.formatted: In line with the multiverse perspective articulated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Steegen et al. (2016)</ref>, future studies should evaluate hypotheses across multiple defensible analytical specifications and integrate the resulting evidence.

text.text: Agreement across approaches strengthens confidence in substantive conclusions, whereas disagreement signals uncertainty.

In the present case, the considerable variation across analytical specifications suggests that firm conclusions regarding prospective relations between work engagement, burnout, and personality traits are not yet warranted.
